title: Short: "The air has a loudest sound"
_source: episodes/S52-air-ceiling/script.md — generated by scripts/script-md-to-json.mjs; edit the .md, not this file. Add 'say' overrides here only via a patch file (episodes/S52-air-ceiling/say.json).

lines.text: Turn a sound up, and keep turning. At some point the air itself says stop.
Air presses on everything around you at about one hundred and one thousand pascals.
A sound is a wiggle on top of that: the pressure goes a little above the line, then a little below, over and over, very fast.
lines.cue: caption: A WIGGLE ON TOP OF THE AIR

lines.text: The quietest reference level on the scale we use in air is twenty millionths of a pascal. The air pressure is about five billion times bigger.
lines.cue: caption: 20 MILLIONTHS OF A PASCAL; 5 BILLION TIMES

lines.text: Fold that into decibels, and the biggest clean sound the air can carry is about one hundred and ninety-four.
That's the ceiling for a sound in sea-level air.
lines.cue: caption: THE CEILING, AT SEA LEVEL

lines.text: Pump in more energy, and you don't get a louder sound. You get something else.
So why does the air have a ceiling, and what happens past it? The full video on our channel has the answer. Like and subscribe so you don't miss the next one.
